nameStory: Squirrel-tail moss gets its charming name from its distinctive branching pattern that resembles a fluffy squirrel's tail. When you see the curved, feathery branches emerging from tree bark, you'll immediately understand why early botanists thought of our bushy-tailed woodland friends. The scientific name 'sciuroides' literally means 'squirrel-like' in Latin, confirming this delightful connection.
description: Squirrel-tail moss is a tree-dwelling moss that forms loose, irregular cushions on bark, creating what looks like tiny green squirrel tails sprouting from tree trunks. The individual plants grow in curved, feathery branches that can reach about an inch long. This moss has a distinctive arched growth pattern, with branches that curve gracefully away from the tree surface. Like most mosses, it's quite small but can form noticeable colonies that catch your eye as you walk through the woods.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, irregular cushions with distinctively curved, arching branches that sweep away from tree bark like tiny feathers or brush strokes

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always grows on tree bark, never on rocks or soil - look for it on the trunks and larger branches of deciduous trees

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels soft and springy when gently pressed, with a feathery quality that's more delicate than cushion-forming ground mosses

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when moist, turning yellowish-green to brownish when dry - the color change is quite dramatic

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny overlapping leaves arranged in rows along the curved branches, giving each 'tail' a scaled appearance like a miniature fern frond

habitat: Squirrel-tail moss grows exclusively on the bark of trees, particularly favoring deciduous species like maples, oaks, and birches in New England's mixed forests. You'll find it on trunk bark and larger branches, usually on the sides that receive some moisture but aren't constantly wet. It tends to prefer trees in partially shaded areas rather than deep forest or completely open locations.

seasonality.spring: Becomes vibrant green as spring moisture returns, with the curved branches looking fresh and plump. This is an excellent time for identification as the distinctive growth form is most pronounced.
seasonality.summer: Remains visible but may appear more yellowish-green during dry periods. The characteristic arching branches maintain their squirrel-tail appearance even when somewhat dried.
seasonality.fall: Often looks its most dramatic as fall rains rehydrate the moss, turning it bright green against colorful autumn bark. Sporophytes may be present on some colonies.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round but appears brownish and contracted. Snow may obscure it, but on mild winter days you can still spot the distinctive branching pattern on bare tree trunks.

funFact: Despite being found around the world, squirrel-tail moss has only been recorded 9 times in all of New England, making it one of our region's botanical mysteries - you might be looking at a moss that fewer than a dozen people have officially documented here!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other tree-dwelling mosses, but the distinctive curved, tail-like branching pattern is unique. Most other bark mosses either form flat mats or upright cushions without the characteristic arching branches that sweep away from the tree surface.
contextualKnowledge: This moss belongs to a small, specialized family of tree-dwelling mosses that have adapted specifically to life on bark. Unlike ground mosses that anyone can easily find, bark mosses like squirrel-tail require careful searching and are often overlooked by casual observers.
compareHints: Squirrel-tail moss is quite distinct from its only New England relative, Leucodon brachypus, which has much shorter, less curved branches and doesn't form the characteristic sweeping 'tail' pattern. While both grow on tree bark, squirrel-tail moss has the more dramatic arching growth that makes it unmistakable once you learn to recognize the pattern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative squirrel-tail moss (Leucodon sciuroides), short-stalked leucodon has much shorter capsule stalks and forms tighter, more compact cushions.
